messages.subject: User-defined distributions: vectorisation
parts:
I notice that the examples of user-defined distributions given in Chapter 11 of the NIMBLE manual are not vectorised. By contrast, in Stan, for example vectorisation is required, and, in general, when writing functions in R I find that vectorisation is an advantage because it reduces the need for for-loops.

My question is: is there any advantage in NIMBLE in vectorising user-defined distribution functions? Currently all my applications are MCMC.

messages.author: bebd85531a67ef86
messages.subject: Re: User-defined distributions: vectorisation
parts: My question is: is there any advantage in NIMBLE in vectorising user-defined distribution functions? Currently all my applications are MCMC.

One advantage is to reduce the number of nodes used to represent the model - this can translate to reducing the CPU time spend to get a model running. e.g. for a time-series, instead of having one node per time step, you might define a vectorised distribution that works with the entire time series (just one node).  In this scenario I would consider vectorising if the CPU time for getting the model running was an issue.

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: User-defined distributions: vectorisation
parts:
To generalize upon David's response: a good way to think about when to vectorize is how having a single vector node vs. many scalar nodes impacts the graph that represents your model.  When an MCMC sampler operates on a node or nodes (the "target"), it must calculate the nodes that depend on the target node(s).   If the part of the model you might vectorize will always need to be calculated together anyway, then vectorizing makes sense.  On the other hand, if one element of what you might vectorize corresponds to one stochastic node updated by one sampler, then it may be better to stay with scalar nodes, so that a sampler for one of the stochastic nodes is not burdened with calculations over the whole vector that are not really necessary.  Does that make sense?

In general, we tend to see much greater gains in MCMC efficiency from customizing the sampling scheme than from re-writing (e.g. vectorizing) the model, but sometimes the latter does indeed help a lot.

A major difference from Stan is that, if I understand correctly, Stan always calculates the entire model, so vectorization where possible is always helpful.  It does not create a graph and then calculate only portions of the model that are needed for particular samplers (as NIMBLE does), because it samples all model states jointly.  While HMC is great, customized sampler configurations in NIMBLE can sometimes be more efficient than Stan.

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: User-defined distributions: vectorisation
parts:
Also one point to remember here is that NIMBLE generates C++ under the
hood, so the R-based motivation for vectorization doesn't hold for
compiled nimbleFunctions. Even aside from Perry's comment about how
vectorization interacts with sampling, whether a vectorized
nimbleFunction is faster than one with a loop depends on the
situation.

chris

messages.author: 78efca6d80693fd9
messages.subject: Re: User-defined distributions: vectorisation
parts:
I had two motives for thinking about vectorisation in this context. The main one was speed, but Christopher's remark about C++ probably undermines the idea that much speed would be gained. My other motive was to simplify the coding. When I looked int0 my model in more detail I realised that it would, in that specific case, vectorisation would not have simplified the coding.

Many thanks to all who responded.
